issues.legal_issue: A public body that requested an acquisition and was adversely affected by an order terminating the acquisition has standing to challenge that order.
material_facts: The land was notified for acquisition at the public body's request and at its expense for construction of a public park.
The public body opposed the landowners’ application to terminate the acquisition proceedings.
The Collector allowed that application, deciding the dispute against the public body.
issues.conclusion: The public body was a person aggrieved by the Collector’s order and had locus standi to challenge it by writ petition.
issues.legal_principle: A person whose request and interests are directly affected by an order deciding a dispute against it is a person aggrieved and may challenge that order. The acquisition was requested under Section 88 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911, and the notifications referred to Section 55 of that Act read with Section 50 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.

predicates.writ_challenging_acquisition_order: The applicant brought a writ petition challenging an order made in an acquisition proceeding.
predicates.applicant_requested_acquisition: The applicant had requested that the land be acquired for a purpose it was responsible for carrying out.
predicates.order_adversely_decided_dispute: The challenged order resolved a dispute against the applicant and adversely affected its interests.

issues.definition: When an applicant that requested an acquisition brings a writ petition against an order that adversely decides a dispute affecting it, the applicant has standing.

issues.legal_issue: A Collector cannot treat acquisition notifications as lapsed merely because possession was not taken within a specified time, and abandonment requires withdrawal by the State Government.
material_facts: The Collector treated the acquisition notifications as lapsed because possession had not been taken within one year of the declaration.
The Collector relied on High Court decisions, including a decision that the Supreme Court had disapproved.
There was no evidence that the State Government had issued a notification withdrawing from the acquisition under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
The Collector’s order did not proceed on the basis that the State Government had withdrawn from the acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The Collector could not drop the acquisition proceedings on the ground that the notifications were deemed to have lapsed; the Collector’s order was unsustainable, and the acquisition proceedings had to continue in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, do not support treating notifications as lapsed merely because possession was not taken within the period relied on by the Collector. The State Government may withdraw from an acquisition under Section 48, but the record contained no such withdrawal. The approach in Radhey Shyam Gupta v. State of Haryana was disapproved in Improvement Trust, Faridkot v. Jagjit Singh and State of Punjab v. Hari Om Cooperative House Building Society Ltd., Amritsar.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns proceedings to acquire land.
predicates.collector_deemed_acquisition_lapsed_for_: The Collector treated the acquisition as lapsed because possession had not been taken within a specified period.
predicates.state_formally_withdrew_acquisition: The State Government formally withdrew from the acquisition.

issues.definition: In a land acquisition proceeding, if the Collector treats the acquisition as lapsed for delay and the State Government has not formally withdrawn it, the Collector cannot terminate the acquisition as lapsed.
